messages.content:
You are the writer of the discussion described below. You write out the discussion that the participants listed below take part in, under the rules and the flow given.

## Setting
Allocating the bicycle parking spaces. A small apartment building has fewer bicycle spaces than residents who want them, and the five members of the residents' association must decide how they are allocated. Participants: Ryuji, Mio, Asuka, George and Shunichi. Each participant has a concern of their own, which the others do not know.
Things that can be looked into (titles only):
- The building account's two-year ledger
- The ward cycle park by the station
- Treasurer's handover file on cash collections
- Trial of the supplier's display frame
- Morning departures watched from the entrance
- Rain exposure along the parking rows
- Five years of association minutes
- Sticker register and the daily riders
- Account from the neighbouring block's secretary
- Last year's complaint log entries

## Discussion format
The talk proceeds in rounds. Each round has 4 turns; in each turn, every participant speaks once, in this fixed order: Asuka, Ryuji, George, Shunichi and Mio. On a turn, a participant either speaks, says "Skip" (passes this turn only), or says "Over" (takes no further turns this round). A participant can address another directly with @Name, to ask them a question, answer theirs, agree with them, or object to what they said. An utterance is anywhere from 1 to 40 words; give it the length and content that suit the moment. An utterance consists only of the participant's own words: no name labels, headings, stage directions or commentary, and no speaking for others. The talk is a conversation among the participants: they respond to one another, asking, answering, agreeing and objecting, and the decision grows out of that exchange.

## Schedule
| Round | Start of the round | Talk | End of the round |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | nothing new (the things that can be looked into are listed above, titles only) | 4 turns | each participant chooses 2 of the listed things to look into |
| 2 | each participant is told what they found out (that participant only) | 4 turns | nothing |
| 3 | everyone is told the options | 4 turns | every participant votes; the option with the most votes is adopted |
- Several participants may choose the same thing; what is found out is told only to the participant who looked into it.
If votes are tied, one of the tied options is chosen by a fixed rule. The discussion ends after the vote.

## Looking into things
After round 1, each participant chooses 2 of the listed things to look into. What they find out is told only to that participant.

## Participants
Name: Ryuji
Age: 28
Gender: male
Personality: Ryuji has a calm and cautious personality, and is the type of person who always assesses the situation before acting. He rarely shows his emotions, and spends his time thinking deeply about many things. His friends consider him to be serious and reliable, but his expressionless attitude can sometimes make them feel uneasy. He tends to judge things based on reason rather than intuition, and strongly sticks to his beliefs. He is very independent and often does things at his own pace.
Concern: Every proposal that comes up at our meetings ends with someone asking what it will cost the building, and nobody has ever gone and looked. I also have no idea what a household actually pays when it ends up with nowhere to keep a bike.

Name: Mio
Age: 17
Gender: female
Personality: Mio has a cheerful and energetic personality that naturally makes those around her smile. She is curious and loves to try new things. She can be a little clumsy at times, but people tend to laugh it off and forgive her when she makes mistakes. She has strong opinions of her own, but is also able to listen to the opinions of others, making her a well-balanced person.
Concern: Whatever we settle on, somebody has to keep it running month after month, and the last two jobs we invented landed on one person and then quietly lapsed. I wanted to know what handling it would actually take, in paperwork and in physical effort.

Name: Asuka
Age: 29
Gender: female
Personality: Asuka has a calm and logical personality, rarely showing her emotions and carefully judging situations. She may seem a little unfriendly at times, but she is very thoughtful and sensitive to her surroundings. She has strong opinions and will assert herself when necessary. She is not very good at socializing, but she is serious about her work and studies.
Concern: Getting a bike out in the morning has turned into a shoving match down there, and where yours happens to end up standing seems to decide what state it is in by the evening. Neither of those is anyone's fault exactly, which is why I went and looked properly.

Name: George
Age: 65
Gender: male
Personality: George has a gentle and calm personality, but he can also be a little stubborn and headstrong at times. He is seen by those around him as a reliable person with a wealth of experience appropriate for his age, and he is always able to make calm judgments, allowing him to handle difficult situations without panicking. However, his expressions sometimes reveal a hint of sternness or awkwardness, and he tends to observe things from a step back rather than actively engaging with others. He is very independent and tends to try to solve problems on his own without relying on others.
Concern: People have started grumbling that the same places always seem to go to the same doors, and I cannot tell whether that is how it actually happened or just resentment. Nor can I say whether the places we have now sit anywhere near where the bikes actually are.

Name: Shunichi
Age: 32
Gender: male
Personality: Shunichi is a very confident person who can remain calm in any situation. He is not modest, and has a slightly sarcastic side, but that is part of his charm. He is not sociable, but he is good at communicating at the right time and is relied upon by those around him. He rarely becomes overly emotional and can analyze situations calmly and act accordingly, so he has an unexpectedly rational side.
Concern: The last thing I want is a rule that turns people who currently nod at each other in the lobby into people who time their exits to avoid it. Things down in the bike area have gone sour once or twice already, and I wanted to know what happens to a building when an arrangement like this starts to bite.

## Hidden information
The options and the full text of every card are listed here. The participants do not know them before the schedule above says so, and nothing from them may appear in the talk before the round in which it is revealed.

Options (see the schedule above):
- A: Paid Allocation. Spaces are attached to a monthly charge and held by whoever takes them up, with the income going to the building's shared account.
- B: Shared Racks. The fixed allocation is dropped in favour of open double-tier racks that anyone may use on arrival, with no space belonging to a particular household.
- C: Annual Lottery. All spaces are drawn by lot once a year among the households that apply, with the result standing until the next draw regardless of circumstances.

Cards (see the schedule above; title: text):
- The building account's two-year ledger: The shared account's ledger for the past two years covers cleaning and lighting and little else, and any capital work would need a levy on households.
- The ward cycle park by the station: The ward cycle park by the station charges 2,600 yen a month, and the notice on its gate listed fourteen households waiting for a place.
- Treasurer's handover file on cash collections: The outgoing treasurer's handover file logs about three hours a month reconciling the small cash collections already run flat by flat, and per-place billing would sit on top of that.
- Trial of the supplier's display frame: On the supplier's display frame, hoisting a loaded bike onto the upper rail took both hands and twenty seconds, and the lift spring needs greasing twice a year.
- Morning departures watched from the entrance: Over two weekday mornings watched from the entrance, eleven bikes left between seven and nine, and on four of those someone had to shift another machine first.
- Rain exposure along the parking rows: The row under the eaves stays dry, but the places past the downpipe take rain across them, and a saddle left there in winter is still wet the next morning.
- Five years of association minutes: Five years of association minutes show the covered places held by the same flats throughout, with no review of the arrangement recorded at any general meeting.
- Sticker register and the daily riders: The building's bicycle sticker register runs from no bikes to three per flat, and the households riding daily, when asked, said they would sooner pay something than be counted as one equal claim.
- Account from the neighbouring block's secretary: At the block behind the building, a monthly charge on places left three households in arrears, and their association secretary said two of them stopped coming to meetings altogether.
- Last year's complaint log entries: The building's complaint log has nine notes from last year about machines leaning on each other, and every one of them died out because there was no one in particular to ask.

Write the complete transcript of the discussion in the exact Markdown format specified. Output only the transcript.

## Output format
Markdown, exactly this structure; nothing before or after it:

# shared_living_0017
## Round 1
### Talk
#### Turn 1 of 4
- **<Name>**: <utterance, or exactly Skip, or exactly Over>
(one line per participant, in the fixed speaking order; repeat for Turn 2, 3 and 4; a participant who said Over has no line in the later turns of that round)
### Action
- investigate: <Name> -> <card title>; <card title>
(one line per participant; titles exactly as listed)
## Round 2
### Talk
(4 turns as above)
## Round 3
### Talk
(4 turns as above)
### Vote
- <voter name> -> <option label>
(one line per participant)
- adopted: <label of the option with the most votes>
## Result
- adopted: <label>
